summary: Egypt lies in the northeast corner of Africa, with the Nile Valley and the heritage of ancient Egyptian civilization, and is one of the most populous countries in the Arab world.

ranking.name: Islam (Sunni)
ranking.description: In 639–642 the Arab general Amr ibn al-As conquered Egypt under Byzantine rule, and over the following centuries, owing to factors such as the poll tax on non-Muslims, intermarriage with the ruling class and social mobility, the people gradually converted to Islam. In 969 the Fatimid dynasty founded Cairo and established the Al-Azhar Mosque (later a university); in 1171 Saladin restored Sunnism, and Al-Azhar has since been one of the most important centers of learning in the Sunni Islamic world.

ranking.name: Coptic Orthodoxy
ranking.description: According to tradition, Saint Mark, author of a gospel, founded a church in Alexandria in the 1st century, and Egypt became a stronghold of early Christianity, with the monastic system also originating here. After the Council of Chalcedon in 451 the Coptic Church split from the churches of Rome and Byzantium, and after the Arab conquest the faithful survived as a minority for a long time to the present. Copts are concentrated mainly in Minya, Asyut and Cairo in Upper Egypt, and in recent years have repeatedly been attacked by extremist groups.

ranking.name: Other Christian denominations
ranking.description: These include the Coptic Catholic Church, evangelical churches formed after American Presbyterian missionary work in the mid-19th century, and historical communities such as the Greek Orthodox and Armenian churches. Most of the Greeks of Alexandria and the Levantine Christians left Egypt after Nasser came to power in the 1950s, so their numbers are small.

religion.background: The polytheistic faith of ancient Egypt lasted for thousands of years; Christianity arrived in the Roman period, Alexandria became the theological center of the early church, and most Egyptians became Christians. After the Arab conquest of the 7th century, Islam gradually became the faith of the majority over several centuries, and the Fatimid dynasty and the later Ayyubid and Mamluk dynasties made Cairo a center of Islamic civilization. Coptic Christians survive to this day as the largest Christian community in the Middle East, and since the 20th century the relationship between religion and politics (such as the Muslim Brotherhood) has been a central issue in Egyptian society.

ranking.name: Arabic (Egyptian dialect)
ranking.description: After the Arab conquest of the 7th century Arabic gradually replaced Coptic, which derived from ancient Egyptian, and became the everyday language of the majority around the 10th–12th centuries. The Egyptian dialect is represented by the Cairo accent and has absorbed vocabulary from Coptic, Turkish, French, Italian and English. In the 20th century Egyptian films, radio and singers (such as Umm Kulthum) swept the Arab world, making the Egyptian dialect the one most familiar to Arabs of every country.

ranking.name: Arabic (Upper Egyptian dialect)
ranking.description: The Upper Egyptian dialect (Sa‘idi) is spoken in the Nile Valley south of Giza as far as Aswan and retains more archaic features, such as pronouncing the letter “ق” as a g sound. Upper Egyptians make up about one-third of the country, and many move to Cairo to earn a living; because of the gap between city and countryside, Sa‘idis are often the butt of jokes in popular culture, but their dialect and poetic tradition (such as the epic of the Hilali) are very rich.

language.history: Ancient Egyptian is one of the earliest languages in human history with written records, passing through hieroglyphs and Demotic to Coptic written in Greek letters. After the Arab conquest of the 7th century Arabic became the language of administration and gradually spread, and Coptic went out of everyday use in the late Middle Ages, surviving only in the liturgy of the Coptic Church. Ottoman, French and British influence brought a large number of loanwords into the Egyptian dialect. Today Standard Arabic is used in writing and formal settings, while the spoken language is the Cairo dialect and the Upper Egyptian dialect.

ranking.name: Koshari
ranking.description: Rice, lentils, short macaroni and chickpeas are mixed together and topped with garlic vinegar and spicy tomato sauce, with plenty of crispy fried onions sprinkled on top.
ranking.history: Koshari is generally thought to have taken shape in the 19th century during British influence in Egypt, and its name may be related to the Indian rice-and-lentil dish “khichdi,” brought by British-Indian soldiers and merchants; the pasta and tomato sauce reflect the Mediterranean immigrant communities of Egypt at the time. Made of cheap grains and legumes, it is nutritious and filling, and became an affordable staple for workers and students. Today Cairo’s streets are full of restaurants specializing in koshari, and it is regarded as Egypt’s national dish.

ranking.name: Ful medames (stewed fava beans)
ranking.description: Fava beans are simmered over low heat for a long time until soft, mixed with olive oil, cumin, lemon juice and garlic, and eaten with Egyptian flatbread; it is the most common breakfast.
ranking.history: Fava beans were already cultivated in ancient Egypt, and remains of fava beans have been found in tombs of the pharaonic era. The word “medames” is generally thought to derive from Coptic, meaning “buried,” describing the medieval practice of leaving a pot of beans overnight in the ashes of a public bathhouse furnace. It is Egypt’s most common breakfast, sold from roadside carts from early morning, and during Ramadan people often eat it at the pre-dawn suhoor meal to keep up their strength.

ranking.name: Molokhia (jute leaf soup)
ranking.description: Chopped jute leaves are cooked in chicken or rabbit broth into a sticky green soup, finished with oil fried with garlic and coriander, and served with rice or bread.
ranking.history: Jute leaves have long been grown in Egypt, and the name is related to the Arabic word for “royal,” with the legend that it was once a court dish. In the early 11th century the Fatimid caliph al-Hakim is said to have banned the common people from eating jute leaves, a history still often mentioned today. It is now one of the most common soups in Egyptian homes; its thick, slippery texture surprises many foreigners, but it is the taste of home for Egyptians.

ranking.name: Ta‘miya
ranking.description: Soaked fava beans are blended with coriander, dill, onion and garlic into a green puree, shaped into small patties, sprinkled with sesame and deep-fried, crisp outside and tender inside.
ranking.history: Egyptian ta‘miya differs from the falafel made from chickpeas elsewhere in the Middle East in that it uses fava beans, so the inside is green. A common explanation is that Coptic Christians, who could not eat meat during the long fasting periods, used bean fritters in place of meat, but the exact origin is hard to establish. It is Egypt’s most common street breakfast, often tucked into bread together with ful medames, and is cheap and almost a daily food for everyone.

ranking.name: Fatta
ranking.description: Crisped flatbread and rice are layered in a bowl, drizzled with garlic vinegar and tomato sauce, and topped with stewed lamb or beef, with a sour, fragrant and rich flavor.
ranking.history: Fatta is a long-established banquet dish of Egypt, and its name comes from the Arabic for “to crumble,” referring to the practice of tearing bread and soaking it in broth. It is most closely associated with the Islamic Eid al-Adha: after slaughtering a sheep or cow, people make fatta from the broth and meat to share with family and give part of the meat to the poor. It is also served at joyful occasions such as the birth of a baby and weddings, a festive dish that symbolizes abundance and sharing.
